Helmet detection results: what we measured

Accuracy, speed, night behaviour and the mistakes we made on the way. Every number says what it was measured on.

Quick answer

After fine-tuning on CCTV frames, recall on held-out frames rose from 0.62 to 0.79 and mAP@50 from 0.55 to 0.75. In the live CCTV worker, about 74% of bare-headed riders were alerted when one frame per second was analysed and about 90% at two frames per second, with about 1% of alerts on fully helmeted bikes. On night-like frames recall is only 0.34, and night training is still to be done.

How we measured

  • Data. The HELMET dataset: 910 clips (100 frames each, 1080p, 10 fps) from traffic cameras in Myanmar, CC BY 4.0. It labels every motorcycle with the helmet state of each person on it.
  • Honest split. We use the dataset's own split. Training used only the training clips; the numbers below come from validation or test clips the model never saw.
  • "Riders caught". For each clip, alerts are compared with the number of bare-headed people in the ground truth; an alert on a bike with a bare-headed rider counts as correct, an alert on a bike where everyone wears a helmet counts as a false alarm. Counts are approximate because the labels name bikes, not individual heads.
  • Limits of the test. One country, daytime, a few hundred riders. Treat the figures as a guide, not a promise for your camera.

1. The model on held-out CCTV frames

500 validation frames, 1,114 riders, from clips not used for training (confidence 0.5, image size 960)
ModelPrecisionRecallmAP@50
First model (public Roboflow data only)0.7770.6170.547
After CCTV fine-tuning0.7980.7910.748

Fine-tuning on a few thousand real CCTV frames matters more than anything else we tried: recall rose by 17 points.

2. The first model on public test sets

Test splits of the public datasets (confidence 0.4, 640 px)
Test setClassPrecisionRecall
Riders and people (300 images)helmet0.930.93
no helmet0.950.84
Caps, hats, hijabs (87 images)helmet0.940.85
no helmet0.870.88

mAP@50 was 0.92 on riders and people and 0.91 on head coverings. Adding head-covering data lifted no-helmet recall on caps and hats from 0.21 to 0.88 without hurting the original set. These sets are easier than real CCTV, which is why the CCTV test above matters.

3. The live CCTV worker at different speeds

The worker analyses as many frames per second as the computer allows. How many riders get an alert depends strongly on that rate. Test: 14 of the busiest held-out clips with 170 bare-headed riders.

1 frame / second
74%
2 frames / second
90%
Same clips, same settings
Analysed frames per secondRiders alertedExtra alerts for the same peopleAlerts on fully helmeted bikes
1about 74%21 (about 1%)
2about 90%441 (about 1%)

Faster analysis catches more riders but also alerts the same person more than once. A repeat filter keeps this in check; a stricter filter removed the repeats but also hid real riders, so we kept it mild.

5. Speed on a CPU, and the trade-off

Test machine: desktop Intel Core i3-10100F, no GPU.

Time per analysed frame and riders caught when frames are 0.5 s apart
Enlarged crops around motorcyclesRiders alertedSpeed
Never81%about 0.3 s per frame
Every 6th frame84%fast
Every 3rd frame85%medium
Every frame90%about 1.3 s per frame

Crops help, but they cost time, and time means fewer frames per second. We run crops on every 5th frame and reach about 1.4 analysed frames per second on this CPU. A GPU or a faster CPU would let us analyse more frames and catch more riders.

6. Night

The same 200 validation frames in daylight and made to look like night (darkened, infrared-style, dusk)
LightingPrecisionRecallmAP@50
Daylight0.800.760.72
Made to look like night0.780.340.31

This was measured before the model saw any night-style images. We have prepared night-style training data, but it is a stand-in; real night footage from your own cameras will help far more.

What went wrong, and what it taught us

  • A result that was too good. Enlarged crops first showed recall 0.86. Looking at the pictures showed giant boxes covering a whole rider and bike. A size check brought recall to 0.76. Always look at the pictures.
  • A tracker built for the wrong frame rate. ByteTrack hid new riders until a second match. At one frame per second most riders never got one, and four of five crowded clips gave no alert. A tracker made for low frame rates fixed it.
  • A filter that was too strict. The first repeat filter removed duplicate alerts but also hid real riders: coverage fell from about 89% to 70%. We relaxed it.
  • A slow training run. Using all mined crops made classifier training take far too long on a CPU. Capping and balancing the data made it practical with no loss in accuracy.
